claims.statement: The credential SOP is that credentials are referenced, never replicated: harnessed never copies, seeds, or snapshots a harness's credential store into a per-stack home, in either backend, because a harness rewrites its own store on token refresh — any copy rots and the next launch restores a stale one, presenting to the user as a silent logout.

Exactly two credential mechanisms are sanctioned: (1) reference the live store via mount or symlink at the real path (ro where the harness only reads, rw where it owns the dir), and (2) reference a token or broker URL via env — no file involved; everything else, including 'copy it back if newer', is replication and out of bounds.

A symlink is a reference only while the harness writes in place: SQLite resolves the link (wal/shm beside the target, one logical DB) so omp's agent.db can be shared by link, but Claude Code replaces .credentials.json on refresh, decaying the link into a stale copy — a property of the harness that decides whether mechanism 1 is available.

launchenv.py defines two shapes of one answer because the backends consume env differently: _resolve_launch_secrets returns ordered --env-file paths (podman needs a file), while _resolve_launch_env returns a KEY->value map applied to os.environ host-side so nothing is written to disk; both read the same sources in the same global→project order, and that shared precedence is why they live in one module.

Every env-file the container path uses is a generated mode-0600 temp: the user's own .env is copied and normalized (surrounding quotes and export prefixes stripped, which podman would otherwise ingest literally), never handed to podman directly, and the caller unlinks the temps once podman has ingested them so resolved values never linger on disk.

_varlock_resolve runs `varlock load --format json` (JSON because podman --env-file keeps quotes literal) memoized per schema dir for one launch's lifetime, forwards an already-set OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN for headless/CI auth, and degrades to 'no secrets from this schema' on failure rather than hard-failing a launch.

varlock load is bounded by a 60-second timeout because it may wait indefinitely on a 1Password unlock approval nobody is present to give (CI, cron, closed desktop app); without it every launch hangs silently on the critical path.

Multi-line secret values are skipped with a warning in the env-file writer rather than written: podman reads a value to end-of-line, so a PEM block would arrive truncated at its first line with the remainder parsed as bogus KEY=VALUE pairs, failing later with no hint of the cause.

_warn_unproxied_secrets is a value-blind readiness report that names only secret NAMES and proxy MODES (safe to run every launch), gated by a cheap text test matching @proxy annotation forms — not prose mentions — so an unclassified or unrouteable secret is named at authoring time instead of surfacing far away as an unexplained 401.

credmounts.py forwards the host's git credential surface as pure podman arg derivation, forwarding sockets and public/config files while never copying private key material: 1Password SSH agent socket as primary SSH_AUTH_SOCK with op-ssh-sign, gpg-agent SSH socket (the YubiKey path, via gpgconf) mounted but claiming SSH_AUTH_SOCK only when 1Password is absent, and colon-containing socket paths skipped defensively.

macOS 1Password agent forwarding is explicitly unverified: a host unix socket does not traverse the host→VM file share, so the module attempts a podman-machine reverse-forward (StreamLocalBindUnlink=yes against stale sockets, ExitOnForwardFailure=yes so a failed forward is never reported as mountable) and on any failure prints a note pointing at the tracking todo and falls back — never blocking or failing the launch.

YubiKey passthrough emits --device args for detected Yubico USB nodes and is Linux-only — macOS's container VM has no /dev/bus/usb, so there the YubiKey reaches the container via the gpg-agent SSH socket relay instead; a missing key or failed lsusb is a clean no-op.

The git identity config (~/.config/git dir, else legacy ~/.gitconfig) is mounted ro because it is a public-key reference carrying user.signingkey/gpg.format=ssh/gpg.ssh.program=op-ssh-sign/commit.gpgsign, while gh's hosts.yml is mounted ro so gh authenticates as the host user — with a warning when the file has entries but no plaintext token, since keychain-stored tokens are unreachable from the container.

The SSH directory is forwarded file-by-file, never as a blanket ~/.ssh mount: config/known_hosts/*.pub always ro, private keys only when the stack's ssh_keys field opts in by basename (single-path-component validated with a re-check that the resolved target stays directly under ~/.ssh), and ssh_keys is honored ONLY from the user's own overlay catalog — a shared repo-catalog stack's private-key declaration is dropped with a warning because the key owner, not a third-party author, must consent.

GPG forwarding covers only the non-secret surface (pubring.kbx, trustdb.gpg, gpg.conf, gpg-agent.conf, sshcontrol) and never private-keys-v1.d/: the prior bash launcher's whole-~/.gnupg mount exposed software-key secret material, and ro does not help because read-only is still exfiltratable by an autonomous agent; SSH-format signing through the forwarded agents is therefore the supported in-container path.

Gating is two-tier: the stack field forward_git_credentials (default off) gates the secret-bearing slice (gh token file, opt-in private keys), but the SSH agent socket plus ro git identity config are auto-forwarded whenever the host agent is live because the socket exposes no key material and gates every use behind a host-side approval/touch — '1Password available → wired up' is the safe default.

CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN (from `claude setup-token`, ~1-year lifetime) is the primary claude auth: it never expires mid-session so no in-container refresh is needed, and when configured no credential file is mounted at all — a token-free ~/.claude.json onboarding stub is mounted separately so the agent skips first-run setup.

A token declared in a resolved --env-file outranks a host shell export: podman -e beats --env-file, so forwarding the host value unconditionally let a stale export outrank every declared source (a per-project token for a different account could never take effect); the launcher withholds the -e forward when any env-file declares the variable, matching the host backend where schema values overwrite inherited shell values.

Token-configured checks resolve every dir and take the LAST declaration (matching podman's last-wins --env-file application over the global→project file order), and an explicit empty string means declared-OFF, not absence: a project-level `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN=` genuinely disables a global token and falls back to the credential file, whereas first-hit answers left the container with no token and no credentials (bd harnessed-7bk).

The legacy per-instance credential seed is acknowledged replication of the host's ~/.claude/.credentials.json into a state-dir copy mounted rw, tolerated only for hosts that have not run `claude setup-token`, warned about with the remedy on every launch, and re-seeded from the host when the copy's expiresAt has passed — the expiry gate exists so a token the container itself refreshed is never clobbered while valid; the underlying refresh race is why this is a fallback, not a mechanism.

isolated_auth: true gives a stack its own Claude identity: the host token is withheld from both supply routes (the -e forward AND _strip_var_from_env_files deleting the variable from the generated env-file temps, since --env-file is passed unconditionally), no host credential is seeded, and a per-instance credentials file is minted in-container by the stack's own /login — not a fourth SOP violation because nothing is copied: the store is the only copy of that credential in existence.

The isolated-auth store lives on the host outside the ~/.claude config volume because _ensure_config_volume destroys that volume whenever the profile fingerprint changes under a 'safe to destroy: credentials are bind-mounted over it and live on the host' invariant — a login stored in the volume would be wiped by the next recipe edit; the store survives ordinary recreates and is cleared only by --fresh, and the flag is claude-only (other harnesses warn and keep the host identity).

The host backend mirrors the claude ladder: with no token, the per-stack .credentials.json is symlinked at the host CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR's copy so refreshes propagate; with a token configured, no link is made, the rescue is skipped, and a leftover per-stack copy is removed — while the user's own shared ~/.claude copy is never deleted.

_rescue_host_credentials runs BEFORE every materialize wipe because _launch_host ends in os.execvpe and never regains control (no exit hook is possible): Claude Code's refresh replaces the .credentials.json symlink with a regular file, so the rescue scans every host home (not just the launching one) for the newest usable copy and promotes it back to the shared ~/.claude file unless that copy is already usable and at least as fresh.

_credentials_are_usable rejects gutted credentials (envelope intact but empty accessToken/refreshToken and zeroed expiresAt) because freshness alone let one emptied file overwrite a working shared token and log out every stack sourcing from it; an expired ACCESS token is deliberately still usable since that is the healthy state a refresh token exists to serve. When a per-stack home is deleted, _scrub_host_home overwrites .credentials.json with null bytes and fsyncs before unlinking, including legacy per-project dirs, so a stranded token is harder to recover.

omp on the container backend rw-bind-mounts the live ~/.omp/agent (auth in the agent.db SQLite store, config.yml, usage, sessions) and runs plain omp — never --profile, which points at an isolated empty store and lands on the login screen; do not 'fix' this shared dir back to isolation by snapshotting, which fragments auth/usage/sessions, resets usage on recreate, and still has to copy most of the dir. Only individual files inside (a regenerated mcp.json, a compat config.yml) are shadowed per-instance.

omp on the host backend uses PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR (an absolute path; PI_CONFIG_DIR is a $HOME-relative name and cannot address one, and --profile is mutually exclusive with the env var and wins) to give the stack its own agent dir, then symlinks agent.db, history.db, sessions/, blobs/ and memories/ at the real store — sound because SQLite writes in place (wal/shm beside the link target), so the replace-on-refresh hazard structurally cannot occur and omp needs no rescue equivalent; a missing host agent.db is skipped with a note and omp prompts a first-run login.

The share-back target honors a user's PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR override only when it points outside harnessed's own homes tree — an inherited override from launching inside another stack's host session names another stack's store, and following it would link a child's shared state at a parent that a rebuild could unlink, leaving a dangling agent.db. Install/setup layers likewise pin PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR and CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR per stack so catalog scripts cannot write into a parent's home.

Secret resolution and 1Password auth are host-only by construction: 1Password app-auth binds the grant to the calling host application and cannot work in-container, and catalog/base/op is a setsid shim that makes the 1Password CLI inside a container fail cleanly ('no accounts') instead of writing its interactive setup prompt to /dev/tty and stealing the agent's keystrokes — while service-account and Connect auth still work unchanged.

Image builds are deliberately credential-free and scanner tokens reach exactly one code path: `_build_derived_image` never touches secrets or varlock, so token-gated scanners (snyk, socket) run only in `_scan_image_in_container` — reached from `harnessed rescan` (also the nightly timer) and re-invoked by `harnessed build` unless --no-security-scans — which resolves tokens host-side via _resolve_launch_secrets(None) (global schema only, project env deliberately excluded), passes them as a mode-0600 temp --env-file, and unlinks it in a finally.

The corporate proxy CA enters builds only as a build secret: the cert lives in the user's harnessed config dir (never the repo) and is passed via --secret to `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=corp_proxy_ca,...` so it is never baked into image history and needs no staging into the build context; at runtime it is an ordinary ro bind mount registered into the container trust store after start.

AWS credentials are forwarded as a broker reference, not a copy: for forward_aws_sso stacks the launcher injects only AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI (the host's aws-sso ECS server via host.containers.internal) plus a bearer token read from the user-owned token file `harnessed aws-sso serve` writes, so the in-container SDK pulls short-lived STS creds over HTTP and no aws-sso binary, store, or SSO token ever enters the container or an image layer.

Recipe `persist: global` entries are default-deny with hard-deny roots — ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.gnupg, harnessed's own config dir, plus bare $HOME — that no allowlist entry can override, so the persist system's deliberate host-dir mounts can never capture a directory the credential machinery treats as a live store.

On the container backend, seed_auth runs after the aborting checks and appends the claude credential mount last, so an early exit can never strand resolved secrets in temp files, and the temp env-files are unlinked in a finally around the podman run whether the launch succeeds or fails.

--fresh performs explicit wipes of persisted in-container auth stores — antigravity's keyring and an isolated-auth stack's own login — because both deliberately survive ordinary pod teardown, so 'start clean' requires the removal to be spelled out rather than inherited from teardown.

The same mcp-remote OAuth token store mount (~/.mcp-auth, rw, whole directory rather than a version subdir) mirrors the claude identity split: host-identity stacks share the host's ~/.mcp-auth while isolated_auth stacks get a per-instance dir, and the store is referenced in place (saveTokens rewrites tokens on refresh) so a consent outlives the pod without anything being copied or seeded.

_VARLOCK_CACHE memoizes _varlock_resolve per resolved schema dir for the lifetime of one CLI process, which is exactly one launch. The safety argument is explicit: one launch must see a CONSISTENT secret set (resolving the same dir twice and acting on different answers would be a bug), and without the memo a single launch pays up to four resolving varlock subprocesses where two suffice — _varlock_resolve_env_file builds the --env-file set, then _claude_oauth_token_configured asks the same dirs, and _resolve_launch_env does both on the host path; tests needing fresh resolution bypass the memo wholesale or call _varlock_cache_clear.

On the container path, the host secrets broker (Topology B) inserts a stage between resolution and the container: launcher._broker_start_for starts one only when launchenv.proxy_schema_dirs(project_path) — a subprocess-free text test for @proxy annotation forms over the SAME global→project dirs _resolve_launch_secrets resolves — is non-empty and --no-secrets is unset; broker.start spawns `varlock proxy start` detached on an ephemeral loopback port with one --path per schema dir, polls `proxy status --format json` for the session whose HTTPS_PROXY names the chosen port, and persists exactly five fields (instance, pod, session, port, cert_dir) — never the endpointToken, placeholderOverrides, or proxy env that `proxy status` also returns — so the state file leaks no secret by construction. A failed start is fatal, with a fixed value-free message naming the instance and --no-secrets.

The pod's route to the broker is pasta's --map-host-loopback,169.254.1.1 (paths.BROKER_HOST_DOOR), composed into the ONE --network value `podman pod create` accepts together with mcp-remote's --host-lo-to-ns-lo and the plain HARNESSED_NET passthrough, and permitted by the egress firewall's ACCEPT of the same literal — three places must agree on it. The door is emitted only when the launch actually got a broker, so no stack is silently handed a route to the host's loopback when nothing is listening there.

Topology B's sanctioned end state is a pod holding placeholders with real values injected on the wire by the host broker, so real values never enter the container env at all; that env flip is issue #439 and has not landed — today even a brokered launch still delivers real values through the unchanged mode-0600 --env-file temps. The opt-out is symmetric: --no-secrets (NO_SECRETS env, truthy 1/true/yes) skips the broker and the pod's proxy wiring entirely while the launch keeps working with the pod holding real values as before; a runtime without pods gets a note and env resolution as before rather than a half-wired broker.

The broker is lifecycle-bound to the pod: it starts BEFORE `pod create` (the pod's network args depend on whether one exists) and is stopped if that create fails; _pod_teardown stops it FIRST and never fatally, because it is a host process holding live secrets that must not outlive the pod — the pod is the containment boundary; and broker.reconcile, run by `harnessed list` before reporting, stops every recorded broker whose pod is gone (corrupt records included), which is the backstop for every teardown path that never ran.

The corporate proxy CA lives at $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/harnessed/corp-proxy-ca.crt (paths.corp_proxy_ca_path — user-owned config dir, never the repo) and is absent by default: all four helpers (_corp_proxy_ca_secret_args, _corp_proxy_ca_mount_args, _install_corp_proxy_ca_in_container, _service_dockerfile_with_ca) probe the file first and no-op — empty arg lists, no exec, no temp Dockerfile — so a machine without the cert builds, launches, and runs services exactly as it would without the feature.

The corp CA enters image builds only as a podman build secret: _corp_proxy_ca_secret_args appends --secret id=corp_proxy_ca,src=<host cert path> to the shared base builds (_build_images_cmd, _build_base_image) and to service image builds, and Dockerfile.harnessed-base consumes it under USER root via RUN --mount=type=secret,id=corp_proxy_ca,dst=/tmp/corp-proxy-ca.crt,required=false (empty-file guard, cp into /usr/local/share/ca-certificates, chmod 0644, update-ca-certificates) — podman streams the file for that one RUN, so the cert is never staged into the build context and never lands in image history, and required=false makes absence a no-op at the Dockerfile layer too.

_service_dockerfile_with_ca injects _CORP_CA_DOCKERFILE_BLOCK — a required=false secret-mount RUN that installs the CA — into a TEMP COPY of a service Dockerfile right after the first complete RUN block (typically the apt-get install that puts ca-certificates on PATH, so subsequent curl/pip/pnpm downloads trust the SSL-inspecting proxy), falling back to after the first FROM when no RUN exists, returning None (standard build, no temp) when the cert is absent or the Dockerfile already mentions corp_proxy_ca, with the caller unlinking the temp.

At run time the corp CA is bind-mounted read-only at /run/corp-proxy-ca.crt — into the agent container's launch mount block and into service containers' hashed create-time argv, so provisioning or removing the cert recreates a sidecar — and _install_corp_proxy_ca_in_container execs as root to copy it into /usr/local/share/ca-certificates and run update-ca-certificates; the agent container's install raises on failure while service containers use best_effort=True (a bounded, swallowed exec — a service base image may lack the ca-certificates package, and even the best-effort path keeps its deadline per test), and on the agent path the install runs after the pod is up and before the egress firewall because the exec is local-only.

harnessed build --corp-proxy-ca-crt <file> is the one-time provisioning path for the corporate proxy CA: it persists the bundle at paths.corp_proxy_ca_path() (creating the config dir if needed and writing the file's text) and every later build — base, agent-derived, or service — auto-uses the persisted file.

The corp CA path is container-only by need: the launch-parity ledger records _corp_proxy_ca_mount_args as 'mounts the CA; the host trusts its own store' and _install_corp_proxy_ca_in_container as 'installs the CA inside a container', because nothing host-side needs help trusting the corporate proxy — varlock resolution, the secrets broker, and the podman build process already run behind the host's installed trust — so harnessed never installs the CA anywhere on the host; the CA is the mirror image of the 1Password constraint, which keeps resolution host-side because it cannot work in a container.
